My question to you is: Were you ever in a position to see or perhaps even hear from other detainees whether detainees were beaten in the interrogation rooms on order of the investigators or on somebody else's orders? In other words, if they were beaten during the interrogation, are you in a position to know who gave that order? Would it be the interrogators or would it be some of the regular camp command? If you know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to those who issued orders for beatings and torture, I don't know who it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: During the interrogations. Well, what time, to your knowledge -- approximately what time would the interrogators go home at night, leave the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until evening time, when they would finish the work and leave. Sometimes they would pass through the restaurant and sometimes not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But it would be --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been by 6.00, half past 6.00. Sometimes earlier, sometimes later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Then am I correct that -- you also testified about hearing cries, seeing people brought out, seeing bodies, dead bodies, the next morning. Did some of these occurrences, the calling out of people, any beatings that you might have seen and told us about, the dead bodies, occur at night-time, after the interrogators had gone home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: My assumption is that it took place during the night, because in the morning we would count the dead bodies. Our daily -- our day would begin with counting the dead. But I apologise. I didn't complete one of my previous answers in response to your first question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could clearly see people being taken from the interrogations, people being carried from interrogations covered in blood and being thrown out on the pista.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But if I understand your prior answer, you were not in a position to know, if a beating occurred during the interrogation, who ordered it, whether it was the interrogator or whether it was some other member of the guard who was in the interrogation room. You said you didn't know; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Now, my last question, if you can. You've just finished recounting again your seeing dead bodies in the morning. You've also told us a number of times when you saw somebody called out or you saw somebody beaten and then you never saw them again. Are you able to tell us the -- not the exact total number of such people who you either saw dead bodies or they disappeared and you never saw them again, but just in a general category, would you say the total during your entire time in the camp would be in the dozens, in the hundreds, in the thousands? I mean, if you took all the people together that you either saw dead or you saw being called out or beaten and never saw again, approximately what would that total be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twenty, 25, sometimes 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That would be -- when you say "25, sometimes 30," you mean for the whole period you were in Omarska or for a lesser period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes on a particular day we would count up to 20. I'm referring to the dead whose bodies were thrown out on the lawn in front of the "white house."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And that occurred every day, just some days, almost every day? Which?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes even more frequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness J, I have three questions for you. In your opinion, what are the characteristics of the voice of Krle? What is it that enables you to identify that voice as his?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first day of my testimony here, I told you that he had been very loud. He was shouting. He was yelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No translation]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the reasons as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, "How could you exactly identify his voice?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My second question, as regards water and food, the detainees and the camp personnel, what kind of water and what kind of food did they have, did they get?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had completely different food. The detainees would receive every day one meal which consisted of a very small piece of bread; some stew, usually bean stew, which had gone bad because of the temperatures, very high temperatures; and a piece -- a leaf or two of cabbage. That was the only meal that we would get in the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, as regards the detainees. What about the camp personnel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: The food was brought to them. It was a different kind of food, cooked food, which was usually brought -- carried through the restaurant. Those were pieces of meat, they had wine, water with ice in it, beer, coffee, very large plates of meat and side dishes. That food was taken to the offices where the interrogations took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I know that you have partly answered my question, my following question, but I will still ask you. Where exactly did they have their food? Where would they eat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: My assumption is that they would eat in the offices where they worked because the food was carried over to them. They wouldn't come down to the restaurant to eat, though from time to time an interrogator would come down to the restaurant and have a beer, for instance. There was a man working in the kitchen with us. He had a kind of work obligation, work duty there. His name was Zoran Delic. So he would bring them some beer or coffee. But they never ate there. I never saw them eating there, any of the investigators, with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Still as regards the food and water, this is what you could observe during the day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was about to answer that question as well. Thank you for reminding me. I said that we had drunk that water, and that water, as far as we heard, was prohibited from use because it was industrial water. It was not potable water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry to interrupt you, Witness J, but my question was, the camp personnel and the detainees, did they drink the same water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the detainees drank the water that you have just described, and what about the camp personnel? What kind of water did they drink?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: The water was brought to them. I saw jerrycans with water near the restaurant, and they drank that water. The water was brought from elsewhere. And on one occasion, a guard told us that it was spring water, natural spring water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask my third question. Do you know individuals, several individuals by the surname or the name of Zigic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew the former secretary of the SUP before the war, Rajko Zigic, who passed away, before the war, and the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Assuming that you have recognised a certain Zigic here, what is it that enables you to distinguish him from the other one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: They do not resemble each other at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, I have a fourth question, which will be the last one. You mentioned an individual by the name of Zoran Delic. When one has to have -- has to do a work obligation, a work duty, be it within the army or within the police, that individual must then wear a uniform or some other type of clothing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: He usually wore a uniform, a former JNA uniform, olive drab in colour, and he always carried a weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But let us imagine if one is performing a security duty, a policeman -- there are individuals who are seconded to perform that kind of task who are detached -- do they have to wear the same clothes as a professional policeman and behave according to the same rules, or is there a difference in their status?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know what type of clothing they should wear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. I just was interested in this work obligation. Witness J, thank you very much. We have come to the end of your testimony here. Thank you once again for coming to the Tribunal, for having had the courage to come here and testify. Let me just wish you a safe journey back to your place of residence, and I hope that you will enjoy life that is still before you. Let me now ask the usher to lower the blinds and show you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At this time we'd like to offer Exhibits 3/116A and B, and 3/117A and B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. Mr. Krstan Simic, I think that you, too, have some documents you would like admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm speaking on behalf of all the Defence counsel and teams. We have no objection to these documents being admitted into evidence. For our part, I should like to offer the following documents. They have already been marked for identification purposes. D30, it is a photograph on which Witness J drew in the positions of certain individuals at the time she looked at the photograph and was watching. The second document is the text that we discussed at length, and we consider that this text is highly relevant, and we shall leave it up to the Trial Chamber to decide and to see the way in which it was taken, because there were a lot of attempts to try and show this document in a different light. There were quotations from the conference. So just one remark there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, just have the documents tendered without any further comment. I don't think that the Defence has in any other documents it wishes admitted into evidence. No? Right. Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm not sure exactly what the second document is. I'm assuming it's the newspaper article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is the newspaper article, Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We, of course, have no objections to the photograph. Your Honour, I think we would object to the newspaper article on the grounds that the witness indicated that, first, when asked specific questions about whether she said a certain thing or not, she indicated that she didn't say that. In addition, based on the questions asked in redirect, it's clear she didn't adopt the article, it was never shown to her, and she can't confirm that any of it was, in fact, her words. So we don't believe that it should be accepted by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber allows the admittance into evidence of the Prosecution documents 3/116, and 3/117, and the Defence asked document 30/1 and 31/1, I think, to be admitted. The registrar has the exact numbers and markings. Mr. Keegan, can you call the other witness now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That would be Witness K.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please have the witness shown in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can we move into closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is necessary because the witness is to be heard in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 8th day of September, 2000, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.07 p.m.,
